# How to Write a Sympathy Note When You Don't Know What to Say

> **In short:** A sympathy note doesn't need to be poetic — it needs to feel like you. Start with a simple "I'm sorry," add one specific memory, and offer one small concrete help. Keep it short. The blank card is the hardest part; once you write the first line, the rest usually follows.

By the end of this guide, you'll have a real, sendable sympathy note — even if you started with nothing but a blank card and a heavy feeling. A note can't fix grief, and it isn't supposed to. It just shows up, and that showing up is almost always enough. This is for anyone who has stared at an envelope and typed and deleted the same line over and over: a friend, a colleague, a neighbor, a person you barely knew but want to acknowledge anyway.

## Before you start
- A card, a piece of stationery, or even a sticky note. Plain paper is fine.
- A real pen. Writing by hand is slower, and slower is better here.
- A quiet 10–15 minutes where you won't be interrupted.
- One small, true memory of the person who died. Anything works.
- The name of the person you're writing to.
- Estimated total time: about 20 minutes from blank page to sealed envelope.

## Step 1 — Pause and pick one true thing to say
The hardest moment is the blank card. Before you write anything, sit for a moment and pick one small, true thing you remember about the person who died. It doesn't need to be profound. Maybe the way they laughed, the cookies they kept on the counter, the chair they always sat in at family dinners. Anything that's real to you. If nothing comes, scroll through old photos or texts for a minute. The point isn't to capture their whole life — just to find one tiny detail that you actually remember.

💬 Example: "She always kept a tin of peppermints in her purse, even in summer."

If your mind goes blank, try writing down three things they did that you can picture clearly. Pick the smallest one. You'll know it worked when you have a small, specific image in your head that feels honest, not impressive.

## Step 2 — Open with a simple, honest line
Write the first sentence of the note. Don't try to be poetic. Don't try to be wise. Just say what you feel in plain words. Most sympathy notes work best when they start with something simple like "I'm so sorry" or "I was heartbroken to hear." Use the name of the person who died if it feels right. The first sentence is the hardest because it's the one that commits you to writing the rest. Once it's on the page, the next part gets easier.

💬 Example: "Dear Sam, I'm so sorry about your dad. I've been thinking about you all week."

If "I'm so sorry" feels too plain, try "I was so sad to hear" or just start with their name. You'll know it worked when the line sounds like something you would actually say out loud, not like a greeting card.

## Step 3 — Add the memory you picked
Write the one small detail you found in Step 1. Make it a sentence or two. Don't explain what it meant — just say it. The reader will feel it on their own. This is the part that turns a generic sympathy card into a real letter, because nobody else in the world will remember that exact thing the same way you do. It's okay if it's silly or small. Silly and small is usually better than trying to be deep.

💬 Example: "I keep thinking about how he always had the right tool in his truck and a coffee in his hand. I never saw him without either."

If writing the memory still feels hard, describe what they did, not how they made you feel. Action is easier than emotion. You'll know it worked when the person who reads it smiles for a second through the hard day.

## Step 4 — Acknowledge the recipient without trying to fix it
Write one sentence that comes alongside the reader, not one that tries to fix their grief. This is the part where most notes go wrong. People write things like "I know how you feel" or "they're in a better place," and almost always those land badly. The person who just lost someone doesn't want to be explained to. They want company. So keep this sentence short and honest, and let it sit beside them.

💬 Example: "I can't imagine what these last weeks have been like. I'm just so sorry you're going through this."

If you don't know what to write here, the safest line is: "I don't know what to say, but I want you to know I'm thinking of you." You'll know it worked when the sentence doesn't try to teach, comfort, or compare — it just stays.

## Step 5 — Offer one small, concrete thing
Add a line with a real offer. The famous "let me know if you need anything" almost never works, because the grieving person has no idea what they need, and asking takes more energy than they have. Instead, name a day, a meal, an errand, or a visit. Make it small enough that they can say yes without thinking. A specific offer is a kind of gift. It tells the reader: I thought about this for more than ten seconds.

💬 Example: "I'm going to drop off a casserole on Tuesday around 5. You don't have to come to the door or even text back."

If you're far away, offer a phone call on a specific day, or a card on a future date (a note one month from now often means more than one right away). You'll know it worked when the offer can be accepted without effort.

## Step 6 — Close warmly and stop
Sign the note. Don't try to wrap it up neatly — they're not expecting a clean ending. A simple "love," "thinking of you," "with care," or just your name is enough. If you don't know the person well, your name alone is fine. The closing is also a good moment to remember that a shorter note is almost always better than a longer one. Two paragraphs is plenty. Three is too many. You don't need to make their grief make sense. You just need to show up on the page.

💬 Example: "With love, Mark" or "Thinking of you, Jen"

If you keep wanting to add more, stop. Send it. You'll know it worked when you feel a small relief — not because the note is perfect, but because it's done and it's real.

## Common mistakes
- **Starting with "I know how you feel."** Even if you do, the line puts the focus on you. Skip it. Try "I keep thinking about you" or "I'm so sorry this is happening" instead.
- **Writing "they're in a better place" or "everything happens for a reason."** These are widely known as the worst lines in a sympathy note. Unless the recipient has specifically told you they believe this, leave it out. Replace with a simple "I'm so sorry."
- **Writing a paragraph about yourself.** Your own grief, your memories, your loss. The note is for them. Keep the focus on the reader or the person who died — not on how their death affected you.
- **Waiting until you find the right words.** There are no right words. A short, sincere note sent on day three is worth more than a perfect one sent never.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Small, sincere notes are how you stay close to people across years. A two-line card today is a stronger tie than a long silence next year.
- **For your business or work:** The same six steps work for condolence notes to colleagues, clients, or employees. Just keep the closing more formal — "With sympathy" or "Kind regards" instead of "Love."
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't write it on the phone. Write it on paper. A handwritten note in the mail arrives like a small act of presence, and it almost always gets remembered.

## Try it now
Pick one person you know who is grieving right now. Find a card or a piece of paper. Spend five minutes and write a first draft using the six steps above. Don't reread it more than twice. Mail it tomorrow.
